stem:
A 9-year-old boy is brought in with several weeks of extreme thirst, frequent urination, weight loss, and fatigue. His blood glucose is markedly elevated and his pancreas produces virtually no insulin.

The underlying process most consistent with his presentation is which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Excess somatostatin suppressing every islet hormone
options.misconception: A regulatory peptide is being elevated to the primary cause.
options.explanation: Somatostatin inhibits insulin and glucagon release, but the classic childhood presentation with absent insulin production reflects autoimmune beta-cell destruction — type 1 diabetes.

options.label: B
options.text: Autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic beta cells
options.misconception: None; type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease of beta cells that abolishes insulin production.
options.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease affecting the pancreatic beta cells, which stop producing insulin; it accounts for under five percent of diabetes cases and requires synthetic insulin.

options.label: C
options.text: Glucagon deficiency from lost pancreatic alpha cells
options.misconception: The counter-regulatory hormone is being blamed for hyperglycemia.
options.explanation: Glucagon raises blood glucose; losing it would lower glucose, not raise it. Absent insulin production from autoimmune beta-cell destruction explains this picture.

options.label: D
options.text: Acquired insulin resistance of his peripheral tissues
options.misconception: The adult-onset mechanism is being applied to a child with absent insulin.
options.explanation: Type 2 diabetes — about 95 percent of cases — is acquired, tied to lifestyle and overweight, and involves tissue resistance to insulin; this boy's beta cells make virtually no insulin, indicating autoimmune type 1 disease.

options.label: E
options.text: Chronic underproduction of ADH by the hypothalamus
options.misconception: Diabetes insipidus is being confused with diabetes mellitus.
options.explanation: ADH deficiency causes dilute urine and thirst without hyperglycemia; this boy has high blood glucose with no insulin production, the signature of autoimmune type 1 diabetes mellitus.

context: Learning objective: separate the two main forms of diabetes mellitus. Type 1: autoimmune beta-cell destruction, no insulin production, under five percent of cases, childhood onset, requires insulin. Type 2: about 95 percent, acquired with lifestyle risk and overweight, driven by cellular resistance to insulin.
